name: Recorded video interview
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: one-way recorded video rounds at JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and IMC. Timed behavioural, motivation and short technical prompts.
description: This models a one-way recorded video round, as firms and candidates describe it. JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and IMC all list or report one, as of Nov 2026. Each prompt is its own paper on its own clock, and a finished paper cannot be reopened. You get 30 seconds to think, then 2 minutes to answer. Prompts 4 and 5 are short technical ones for researchers and strats, with 90 seconds to answer. Both state every fact they need. The app does not record you. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend, in one take. Then mark each answer against its rubric from the recording. Each answer needs 7 of 10, with its time row ticked. Two checks at the end ask for what the app cannot see.

items.title: The hardest part
items.prompt:
Thinking time 30 seconds, then answer time 2 minutes, in one take. When the thinking time is up, press Start the clock and speak. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend. The paper ends when its clock reaches zero.

**What do you expect to find hardest in a quant internship, and how are you preparing for it?**
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape. It is 147 words, about 68 seconds at 130 words a minute.*

The hardest part will be speed: correct code on real data while the questions keep changing. At university my code is marked once, a week later. On a desk, a slow answer is a late answer. So I have been training for that. Each week I solve 20 timed problems, with a 25-minute limit on each. Over six weeks that is 120 problems. My median time has fallen from 31 minutes to 19. I also rebuilt one project in pandas from a blank file, without my old notes. It took two evenings, not one, and that showed me where my gaps were. I expect the first month to feel slow anyway. I will ask for one piece of feedback each Friday and act on it the next week. I still want this work because the feedback is fast and honest. That is what will make me better.

rubric.text: Names one hard thing in the first sentence
Says why it is hard for you, from your own experience
Says what you are doing about it, with a number such as problems, hours or weeks
Ties the hard thing to the daily work of the role
Closes on why you still want the role
Finishes before the 2:00 answer clock reaches zero
Uses three or fewer filler words such as "um", "like" or "you know", counted from the recording

items.title: A mistake in someone else's numbers
items.prompt:
Thinking time 30 seconds, then answer time 2 minutes, in one take. When the thinking time is up, press Start the clock and speak. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend. The paper ends when its clock reaches zero.

**Tell us about a time you found a mistake in someone else's numbers. What did you do?**
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape. It is 144 words, about 66 seconds at 130 words a minute.*

I once found an error in a teammate's returns table, and I raised it before our deadline. In a second-year project, four of us wrote a report on two funds. My teammate averaged two daily returns to get the two-day return. One fund rose 10% and then fell 10%, and the table showed 0%. I compounded it instead: 1.1 times 0.9 is 0.99, so a 1% loss. Before saying anything, I rechecked it on three other pairs of days. All three were off in the same direction. Then I messaged him privately with one worked example, not a list of faults. He fixed the formula in ten minutes, and we reran every table. We handed in a day early and scored 74%. I learned to show the check, not just the claim. Now I add one compounding test to every returns sheet I build.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: whose mistake, and that you raised it
Gives the situation in at most two sentences
Says at least two things you did, with "I", not "we"
Says how you checked the mistake before you raised it, and how you raised it
Gives a result with a number
Ends on one thing you now do differently
Finishes before the 2:00 answer clock reaches zero
Uses three or fewer filler words such as "um", "like" or "you know", counted from the recording

items.title: More work than time
items.prompt:
Thinking time 30 seconds, then answer time 2 minutes, in one take. When the thinking time is up, press Start the clock and speak. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend. The paper ends when its clock reaches zero.

**Tell us about a week when you had more work than time. What did you drop, and why?**
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape. It is 143 words, about 66 seconds at 130 words a minute.*

In one exam week I had 12 hours of work and 9 hours free, so I dropped the newsletter. I had an essay worth 40% of a module and a problem sheet worth 10%. I also edit the newsletter, which carries no marks. I listed each task with its hours: the essay 6, the sheet 3 and the newsletter 3. Marks per hour were about 6.7 for the essay, 3.3 for the sheet, 0 for the newsletter. So the newsletter went first. I asked the society chair to run a short edition that week, which saved my 3 hours. That left 9 hours of work for 9 hours free. The essay scored 68%, my best mark that year. The newsletter went out two days late, and the chair told readers why. Next time I would list the hours on Monday, not on Wednesday.

rubric.text: Answers in the first sentence: what you dropped
Gives the tasks and their hours or weights, as numbers
Gives the rule you used to choose, such as marks per hour
Says what you told the person affected
Gives the result with a number
Says what you would do earlier next time
Finishes before the 2:00 answer clock reaches zero
Uses three or fewer filler words such as "um", "like" or "you know", counted from the recording

items.title: One hundred signals
items.prompt:
Thinking time 30 seconds, then answer time 90 seconds, in one take. When the thinking time is up, press Start the clock and speak. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend. The paper ends when its clock reaches zero.

**A colleague tests 100 trading signals at the 5% level. None has a real edge. Explain how many will look significant, and what you would do before trusting one.**
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape. It is 139 words, about 64 seconds at 130 words a minute.*

About 5 of the 100 will look significant by chance alone. A signal with no edge still passes a 5% test one time in 20. So 100 tests give 100 times 0.05, which is 5 false finds on average. The chance that at least one passes is 1 minus 0.95 to the power 100, about 99.4%. So one significant signal out of 100 tells us almost nothing. Before trusting one, I would do three things. First, raise the bar for the number of tests: a Bonferroni cut-off is 0.05 over 100, so 0.0005. Second, test the best signal on data it has never seen, such as the last two years held back. Third, ask whether there is a reason for the effect, not only a p-value. If it survives all three, I would trade it small and watch it.

rubric.text: The first sentence gives the number: about 5 of the 100
Says why: each signal with no edge passes a 5% test one time in 20, so $100 \times 0.05$
Says at least one false pass is almost certain: $1 - 0.95^{100}$, about 99.4%
Names a fix for many tests, such as the cut-off $0.05 / 100 = 0.0005$ or a false discovery rate
Names a check on data held back from the search
Finishes before the 1:30 answer clock reaches zero
Uses three or fewer filler words such as "um", "like" or "you know", counted from the recording

items.title: Twenty comparisons
items.prompt:
Thinking time 30 seconds, then answer time 90 seconds, in one take. When the thinking time is up, press Start the clock and speak. Record yourself on your phone, or answer to a friend. The paper ends when its clock reaches zero.

**Explain why binary search finds a price in a sorted list of 1,000,000 prices in at most 20 comparisons. What goes wrong if the list is not sorted?**
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape. It is 138 words, about 64 seconds at 130 words a minute.*

Twenty is enough because each comparison halves the part of the list that can still hold the price. We look at the middle price first. If ours is smaller, the whole top half is ruled out at once. After one comparison 500,000 prices remain, after two 250,000, and so on. Twenty halvings divide by 2 to the 20, which is 1,048,576. That is more than a million, so 20 comparisons always finish. Nineteen are not always enough, because 2 to the 19 is only 524,288. A scan from the start could need all 1,000,000 comparisons, 50,000 times as many. The catch is the sorting. On an unsorted list, ruling out half is not safe, so the search can miss the price. Sorting first costs about $n \log n$ steps, so it pays only when we search many times.

rubric.text: The first sentence gives 20 and the halving reason
Shows the halving with numbers: 500,000, then 250,000
Compares with a scan of up to 1,000,000 comparisons
Says the list must be sorted, and what goes wrong otherwise
Finishes before the 1:30 answer clock reaches zero
Uses three or fewer filler words such as "um", "like" or "you know", counted from the recording
